content: Familial hypercholesterolemia is a common inherited metabolic disorder that follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. This means that individuals who are heterozygous (carriers) for the condition are affected, while those who are homozygous experience a more severe form of the disease. The global prevalence of heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is estimated to be at least 1 in 500 individuals, though recent genetic studies from Denmark and next-generation sequencing data suggest the prevalence may be closer to 1 in 250. In children, the diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia is based on elevated levels of total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, DNA-based analysis, or a combination of these methods. Coronary atherosclerosis has been observed in men with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia as early as 17 years of age and in women by 25 years of age. Due to the premature onset of atherosclerotic complications, particularly in males, lifelong treatment initiated during childhood is essential to mitigate the risk of cardiovascular disease. Historically, dietary modifications were the primary treatment for children with familial hypercholesterolemia. However, the introduction of lipid-lowering medications has significantly improved treatment outcomes. Anion exchange resins, such as cholestyramine and colestipol, were effective but poorly tolerated by patients. Since the 1990s, studies involving children aged 6 to 17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia have demonstrated substantial reductions in serum total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol levels with the use of statins. While statins appear to be safe and well-tolerated in children, their long-term safety in this population has not been definitively established. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of statins in children with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. Relevant studies were identified through systematic searches of the Inborn Errors and Metabolism Trials Register and Medline, with the most recent search conducted on November 4, 2019. The inclusion criteria were randomized and controlled clinical trials involving participants up to 18 years of age, comparing statins to placebo or dietary interventions alone. Out of 26 potentially eligible studies, nine randomized placebo-controlled trials involving 1,177 participants were included. The duration of intervention and follow-up was generally short, with a median of 24 weeks (ranging from six weeks to two years). Statins were found to significantly reduce mean LDL cholesterol concentrations at all time points, based on high-quality evidence. There was little to no difference in liver function markers (serum aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and creatinine kinase levels) between the statin and placebo groups, according to low-quality evidence. Similarly, there was little to no difference in the incidence of myopathy (as measured by changes in creatinine levels) or clinical adverse events, based on lowto moderate-quality evidence. One study on simvastatin suggested a slight improvement in flow-mediated dilation of the brachial artery (low-quality evidence), while another study on pravastatin over two years indicated a potential regression in carotid intima-media thickness (low-quality evidence). No studies reported cases of rhabdomyolysis (a severe breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue), deaths due to rhabdomyolysis, quality of life outcomes, or adherence to study medications. In conclusion, statin therapy is an effective lipid-lowering treatment for children with familial hypercholesterolemia, with few or no significant safety concerns identified in the short term. However, the long-term safety of statins in this population remains uncertain. Children receiving statin therapy should be closely monitored by their pediatricians, and care should transition to an adult lipid specialist once they reach 18 years of age. Large, long-term randomized controlled trials are necessary to address the unresolved questions regarding the long-term safety of statins in children.
